## Mulhacén at 3,479 m: High Mountain Climate on the Horizon

From the viewpoint of Capileira, at 1,436 meters, Mulhacén stands out against the sky with a presence that belies the mildness of the climate experienced below. The road ends in the village, but the view continues to ascend across slopes that change in color and thermal logic. What the visitor perceives as a photogenic backdrop is, in climatic terms, another planet: the nival zone, where average January temperatures hover around three degrees below zero and annual precipitation reaches 1,500 millimeters, according to records from the Sierra Nevada reference station located at 2,500 meters.

This station, managed by the Sierra Nevada Global Change Observatory, has been measuring a climate for decades that has no equivalent anywhere else in the province of Granada. While winter thermometers in Órgiva rarely drop below five degrees above zero, on the peaks crowning the Alpujarra, the cold sets in for months with a persistence that conditions all ecological processes. Snow there is not an exceptional episode, but a prolonged state that defines water availability, plant survival, and the very morphology of the terrain.

Mulhacén, with its 3,479 meters, acts as a moisture condenser that intercepts Atlantic and Mediterranean fronts. Moist air masses ascend the southern slope and cool as they gain altitude, discharging precipitation that in winter is almost always in the form of snow. This mechanism explains why the Alpujarra, situated at a latitude where arid and semi-arid climates predominate, can sustain irrigation ditches, chestnut trees, and irrigated agriculture that depends entirely on the spring melt.

Data from the Global Change Observatory adds a layer of urgency to this description. The permafrost of Mulhacén's rock glaciers has degraded by thirty percent since the year 2000, a figure researchers interpret as an early indicator of deeper transformations. Rock glaciers are accumulations of rock fragments cemented by underground ice, and their progressive thawing alters slope stability and the hydrological dynamics of high basins.

Permafrost degradation is not an abstract phenomenon of interest only to geomorphologists. It has direct consequences on the flow of rivers descending towards the Alpujarra villages, especially during the low-water months, when the melting of perpetual snow and underground ice constitutes the main water reserve. If that reserve diminishes, the network of irrigation ditches that structures the agrarian landscape of the region loses one of its most reliable sources of supply.

The contrast between the high mountain climate and that of the villages situated on the mid-slopes is also manifested in the vegetation. Above 2,800 meters, even the hardiest brooms and grasses disappear, giving way to a mineral landscape where only a few lichens colonize the rocks. This biological boundary, known as the cryomediterranean zone, represents the upper limit of plant life in the Iberian Peninsula and constitutes a natural laboratory for studying ecosystem responses to global warming.

Fieldwork carried out under the auspices of the Observatory has documented an upward altitudinal shift of several plant species over the last two decades. Plants that once found their ecological ceiling at 2,400 meters now appear at 2,600 or 2,700 meters, displaced by rising average temperatures. This movement, imperceptible to the occasional visitor, reveals constant pressure on summit habitats, which see their available space reduced as thermal conditions become milder.

Snow, the undisputed protagonist of winter in the peaks, also shows signs of change. Records from the reference station indicate a reduction in the duration of the snow cover, which settles later and disappears earlier than in previous decades. For the municipalities of the high Alpujarra, accustomed to living with snow as just another element of the agricultural calendar, this alteration modifies the rhythms of sowing, irrigation, and grazing that have structured life in the region for centuries.

Mulhacén is not just a peak to be admired from the viewpoints of Capileira or Trevélez. It is a climate archive that records, in its snowfields, its rock glaciers, and its plant communities, the changes that are redefining the relationship between the mountain and the villages that live at its feet. The extreme Alpujarra does not end at the last village on the road: it continues upwards, into a territory where the climate is measured by other parameters and where the future is written in degrees of temperature and centimeters of accumulated snow.

The reference station at 2,500 meters provides a continuous window into that vertical world. Its sensors record air temperature, wind speed, solar radiation, and snowpack thickness every hour, generating time series that allow the present to be compared with the recent past. This information, accessible to scientists and managers of the Sierra Nevada National Park, forms the basis upon which decisions are made regarding public use, the conservation of threatened species, and hydrological planning for the Guadalfeo basin.

The visitor ascending from Capileira to the Poqueira refuge, at 2,500 meters, traverses in just a few hours all the climatic zones that separate the Mediterranean world from the nival world. This journey, which can be completed on foot in a demanding day, offers a lesson in physical geography more eloquent than any textbook. Wild pine forests give way to broom scrub, and these to scree slopes and snowfields, in a sequence that compresses into a few horizontal kilometers a thermal gradient equivalent to that which separates Andalucía from Scandinavia.

This vertical compression is the essence of the extreme Alpujarra. In less than forty kilometers in a straight line, the traveler can go from the 300 millimeters of annual precipitation in Órgiva to the 1,500 in the peaks, from the mild temperatures of the valley to the polar winters of Mulhacén. Four climates, four ways of life, and four ways of inhabiting the territory coexist in one of the regions with the greatest environmental diversity in the Iberian Peninsula.
